H. Challenges and Limitations of RAG
Although Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) improves
LLM outputs by integrating external data, it faces signifi-
cant challenges such as relying on the quality of retrieved
documents, continued hallucinations, and high computational
demands for embedding, indexing, and similarity search [1]–
[4], [15], [24], [61], [62], [74]. Evaluation and benchmarking
are still problematic due to a lack of defined measures, lan-
guage biases towards high-resource datasets, and insufficient
frameworks for distinguishing retrieval from creation mistakes
[6], [63], [70]. Domain adaptability and transparency are also
limited, particularly in culturally specialized domains such as
Philippine history, where structured sources are few and source
attribution is frequently insufficient, reducing reliability and
confidence for educational purposes [66], [81]. I. Rag applications in Student Learning

E. Vector Store
The embedded text chunks are stored in an FAISS vec-
tor database, which supports efficient similarity search over
high-dimensional embeddings and enables large-scale retrieval
with minimal latency. Cosine similarity is employed using
L2 normalization and inner product search to ensure that
similarity comparisons emphasize semantic alignment rather
than vector magnitude. A flat index structure is used to guaran-
tee accurate nearest-neighbor retrieval. LangChain’s document
store maintains mappings between vector identifiers and their
original text segments, allowing the system to reconstruct the
appropriate context for the language model.
